context: Al-Hujurat is Medinan and belongs to the later years, when Madinah had become the centre of a state and delegations were arriving from tribes across Arabia. The rooms it is named for are the small dwellings of the Prophet's ﷺ wives, built against the mosque wall, and some of the arrivals stood outside them and shouted for him.

Because the setting is a crowded city rather than a besieged minority, the surah's subject is speech: who speaks first, how loudly, and about whom. Five of its verses open by addressing the believers, each introducing a rule about the tongue or the ear, and verse 13 widens the address to all humanity.
name_story: The hujurat are the rooms in which the Prophet's ﷺ wives lived, adjoining the mosque in Madinah, and the name is taken from verse 4, where men call to him from behind them instead of waiting until he comes out. Naming a surah for a domestic detail fixes its scale: not doctrine, not warfare, but the noise a man makes at another man's door.

movements.note: Believers are told not to put themselves ahead of Allah and His Messenger, not to raise their voices above his, and not to call to him from outside his rooms.
A report brought by a corrupt person must be checked, in case a people is harmed in ignorance and the harm regretted afterwards.
Where two parties of believers fight, the rest must reconcile them and act against the aggressor until it returns to Allah's command. The rule rests on one sentence: the believers are but brothers.
Mockery, insult, nicknames, suspicion, spying and backbiting are prohibited in turn, the last of them given an image instead of an argument, since the backbiter eats his dead brother's flesh.
Descent is stated as a means of recognition and not a rank, and bedouins who announced that they believed are told to say instead that they had submitted.
Faith is defined by what it produces, belief that does not afterwards doubt and striving with wealth and self, and the surah ends by declining to accept Islam as a favour done to Allah.

themes.d: These prohibitions arrive in the same imperative form as the rulings on fighting and reconciliation, which places a rumour and a nickname among the things a Muslim answers for.
Verse 6 ties verification to a consequence, harming a people in ignorance and regretting it later. The obligation falls on whoever hears the report, not only whoever started it.

The statement that believers are brothers arrives inside instructions for what to do when they are fighting, so it generates duties for third parties. Jurists built the law of rebellion on verse 9 and differ over its conditions.
The closing passage separates the outward act of submission from faith settling in the heart. It does not deny the bedouins' Islam; it declines to let them assess their own standing.

heart: Recited slowly, Al-Hujurat is uncomfortable in a particular way, because almost everything it forbids is ordinary. Nobody sets out to backbite. The surah names small acts that people perform without deciding to, then attaches them to the same authority that governs prayer and fasting.

Repeated reading also slows a person at verse 13, which is quoted often and read quickly. It does not abolish lineage but gives it a function, recognition, so that what a person carries from family, colour or tribe stands as description and not as merit. The criterion put in its place is one no reader can measure in anyone else.

passages.why: The verse that makes verification a duty, naming both the kind of report that triggers the rule and the harm it prevents.
Suspicion, spying and backbiting in one verse, with the image of eating a dead brother's flesh placed where it cannot be argued with.
The one address to all humanity here, and read alongside verse 11 it explains why mocking a people was forbidden two verses earlier.
The difference between saying we have believed and saying we have submitted, useful when weighing one's own claim rather than another's.

connections.why: An-Nur legislates after a false report nearly tore Madinah apart, and Al-Hujurat states the rule that would have stopped it: the case and the principle.
Al-Munafiqun treats faith claimed by the tongue and absent from the heart in its dangerous form; Al-Hujurat treats the same gap when it is merely premature.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Al-Hujurat. What is authentically recorded is an occasion: Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, a companion with a loud voice, feared after verse 2 came down that his deeds had been nullified, and the Prophet ﷺ sent word that he was a man of Paradise. That report, in Bukhari and Muslim, concerns the revelation and not a reward for reading. The surah's standing rests on its content, the Qur'an's most concentrated body of rulings on speech.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; occasion for 49:2 in Bukhari and Muslim
